source.title: Anatomy of a failure: When, how, and why deep vision fails in scientific domains
source.authors: Ji-Hun Oh; Dou Hoon Kwark; Kianoush Falahkheirkhah; Kevin Yeh; John C. Cheville; Volodymyr V. Kindratenko; Rohit Bhargava

record.tranche_reason: The study reports its own results on pruning a hard training subset used as an approximation to memorized examples. It refines the simple claim that removing memorized examples lowers test accuracy: the reported test effect differs between IR and H&E models.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports train–test gaps, cue sensitivity, spatial downscaling, dimensionality, and robustness-method results. Rows for those findings are recorded under fits_no_version because they do not measure the behavior named by V1–V7. Cited findings from other work are not recorded as results.
record.test_reason: The Monte Carlo dropout experiment bears on V6 in a new scientific-imaging setting. The hardness-based pruning experiment does not establish V8: examples were selected by difficulty rather than individual memorization effects, and removal was not compared with equal-sized random removal.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. The authors attribute IR underperformance to simplicity bias favoring shallow spectral cues and suppressing spatial learning. Hard-subset pruning improves IR test accuracy while H&E performance stays relatively stable. They acknowledge approximate memorization measurement, setting dependence, and possible H&E-derived annotation bias.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses patient-wise train/test folds and a ResNet50 trained from scratch via ERM on tumor labels; for the memorization analysis it prunes a hardness-ranked subset, rather than fitting random labels or applying the original inclusion-based procedure to each example.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported gap varies by image domain (H&E, IR, virtual H&E) and metric (accuracy, AUROC, AUPRC).

fits_no_version.finding: Removing the hardest 5% of training examples improves IR test accuracy by 2.36%; H&E test performance remains relatively stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hardness-based data pruning can improve IR classification without a corresponding H&E improvement in this setting.

fits_no_version.finding: Both domains exhibit inclusion-dependent accuracy on the hard subset, with greater estimated memorization in H&E.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Subset-based memorization estimates differ between matched IR and H&E classifiers.

fits_no_version.finding: IR has larger train–test gaps than H&E and virtual H&E across accuracy, AUROC, and AUPRC.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The baseline ResNet50 generalizes less well on IR than on matched H&E representations in this prostate-tissue task.

record.problems: The dataset is a subset of a larger cohort, and the authors say full cohort and acquisition details will be reported elsewhere. Memorization is estimated by pruning the top 5% hardest samples rather than by exact leave-one-out retraining. The supplied results give no random-removal comparison for the pruning experiment.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional accuracy and robustness-method results in Tables 2 and 3, plus figure-based cue, downscaling, representation, and uncertainty results. These do not test V1–V8 as defined, so they are not included as rows. The table results and figure descriptions are in §§2.5–2.7 and Figs. 2–4.

untested.parts: No fixed-random-label training and natural-label comparison.
No width sweep across the zero-training-error threshold.

No controlled convolutional versus fully connected comparison on the same image inputs; spatial collapse changes the information available, and MLP-Mixer is not the specified fully connected baseline.
No controlled batch-size comparison under fixed epoch budgets.
No training-set-size or dropout-rate sweep, no joint dropout/weight-decay removal experiment, and no isolation of training-time dropout from stochastic inference averaging.
No magnitude-aware weight-perturbation sharpness measurements or ranking against competing generalization measures.
No comparison of removing individually high-memorization examples against removing an equal number of random examples.

missing.what: Add the V6 Monte Carlo dropout comparison: IR baseline accuracy 76.4%; MCD accuracy 79.1±7.3%, reported as +2.7 points. Head dropout p=0.5 is applied during training and inference, averaging five forward passes. This result was incorrectly excluded as unrelated robustification performance.

record.verdict_notes: The supplied text contains no readable figure values beyond its prose and tables. The hardness procedure explicitly risks removing distribution-level patterns, so its pruning results cannot adjudicate V8's memorization-specific comparison. Limited gains from dropout still support V6's modest claim; failure to reach H&E accuracy does not challenge it.

versions.untested_parts: The study prunes the top 5% hardest training samples as a subset-based approximation; it does not identify individual examples using the exact inclusion-based criterion in V8 or compare removal against an equal-sized random subset.

relationships.condition: IR ResNet50 with head dropout p=0.5 during training and inference, averaging five stochastic predictions
relationships.reason: Text-based verdict; missing row: Table 3 reports 79.1% test accuracy versus 76.4% for baseline, a 2.7-point gain. This supports the combined Monte Carlo dropout recipe; dropout's isolated contribution is unresolved.
relationships.display_finding: Higher test accuracy was reported when dropout training was combined with averaging stochastic predictions. The comparison remains unverified and cannot establish whether the gain came from dropout, stochastic prediction averaging, or both.
